opus-5.5.text:
Well, I'd frame it a bit carefully. It's not that I think policy work is doomed or that people shouldn't do it. It's that when I look at the space, I see a lot of ways to do harm that are easy to miss, and relatively few interventions where I feel confident the sign is positive.

Part of it is that we're very early. We don't have a clear picture of what AI systems will look like in five or ten years, what the key risks will turn out to be, or what good regulation would even consist of. When you're that uncertain, it's easy to push for something that sounds reasonable now and turns out to be counterproductive later. You might lock in a framework built around the wrong threat model, or give people a false sense that the problem is handled.

Then there's the question of who ends up wielding whatever you build. You might advocate for more government involvement, picturing careful, safety-focused oversight. What you actually get could be something that mainly accelerates a race, say between the US and China, or that entrenches particular actors, or that gets captured by interests that don't share your goals. Policy is a very lossy channel. You put an idea in, and what comes out the other end has gone through a lot of politics.

There are also reputational and polarization dynamics. If people concerned about AI risk come across as alarmist, or get associated with one political faction, or push for something heavy-handed that backfires, that can poison the well for a long time. It can make it harder to get serious measures adopted later, at the point when we actually know more and they're actually needed.

So my general view has been that for a lot of people, the priority should be building knowledge, relationships, and credibility, and getting into positions where they can be helpful when the moment comes. That's in contrast to pushing hard on specific proposals now. And when people do act, they should be thinking about downside risk at least as much as upside. That said, my views have shifted somewhat as things have moved faster and some clearer opportunities have emerged. I wouldn't say "don't touch policy." I'd say go in with a lot of humility about how hard it is to know whether you're helping.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I want to be careful here, because I don't think the expected value of working on AI policy is negative. I actually think it's one of the more promising things people can do. But I do think it's an area where the variance is really high, and where it's unusually easy to do harm while feeling like you're doing good.

Part of it is just that we don't know what we want. If you ask me, "What should the US government do about AI right now?" I can give you some things I'm fairly confident about, like better visibility into what frontier labs are doing, or investing in evaluations and security. But a lot of the big-ticket proposals people throw around, things like "pause everything" or "nationalize the labs" or "pass sweeping licensing regimes," I genuinely don't know whether those make the world better or worse. And policy, once it's in place, tends to be sticky. You can lock in a regulatory framework in 2024 that's built around the wrong threat model, and then that framework is still there in 2034 shaping everything, and it's very hard to undo.

The second thing is that policy is adversarial and political in a way that, say, technical safety research mostly isn't. If I do some alignment research and it turns out to be useless, well, that's a wasted few years, but the world isn't worse. If I push hard for a policy and it turns out to be a bad idea, I haven't just wasted my time. I may have polarised the issue, burned credibility, created a backlash, or associated the whole idea of AI safety with something that looks silly or self-serving in hindsight. There's a real dynamic where a clumsy early intervention makes the good later intervention harder.

And I think there's a specific failure mode I worry about, which is people with very strong views about how the future goes, who are very confident, and who get into positions of influence and then push for things that are premised on their particular picture being right. If you look at the history of people trying to shape high-stakes technologies through policy, confidence has not been a great predictor of being correct. So I'd rather see people go in with a kind of humility, where the goal is to improve the quality of decision-making, build up state capacity, get better information flowing, and preserve options, rather than to win a specific fight right now.

So the way I'd put it is: the downside tail is fat. Most people working on this will probably do something between mildly positive and neutral. But a few actions could be quite negative, and it's not always obvious in advance which ones those are. That's a reason to go in, but to go in carefully, to prioritise being right over being loud, and to be pretty suspicious of yourself when a policy you favour also happens to be one that makes you or your allies more powerful.

astra-6.text:
I think the basic issue is that it’s very hard to know what you want policy to do. It’s one thing to say, “AI could be enormously consequential, and governments should take that seriously.” It’s another thing to identify a particular intervention that would actually make things go better.

You could have a policy that sounds like it’s promoting safety, but in practice it makes it harder to do useful safety research. Or you could raise awareness of how powerful AI might become, and the main effect is to get governments more excited about competing to develop it first. So even if you’re right about the importance of the issue, that doesn’t tell you whether your intervention has the right sign.

And policy is an area where you can create effects that are difficult to undo. You can get an issue associated with a particular political faction, or establish a regulatory approach that persists even after you learn that it wasn’t the right approach.

So I wouldn’t say the conclusion is that nobody should work on AI policy. I’d say there’s a big difference between building expertise and relationships so that you’re in a position to help, and pushing hard for a specific change. For the latter, I think you need a pretty strong understanding of both the technology and the institutions involved, and a concrete story about why the change will help.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I think a lot of it comes down to how little we understand about what good policy would actually look like. It’s much easier to say, “AI could be enormously consequential, so we should get policymakers involved,” than it is to identify a particular thing they should do that would reliably make the situation better.

For example, you might raise awareness of how powerful AI could become, hoping that this leads to more caution. But it could instead lead governments to think, “This is a critical national security technology, and we need to get there before anyone else.” Then you’ve increased the pressure to race, and possibly made cooperation harder. That’s a pretty different outcome from the one you were aiming for.

There’s also a risk of locking in an approach too early. If you get a particular framing or regulatory framework established, it can be hard to change, even as you learn more about the technology and what the actual problems are.

So I wouldn’t say the conclusion is that nobody should work on AI policy. I’d say that having a good intention and a plausible story about how your intervention helps isn’t enough. You need to think quite hard about the other effects it could have. And I’m generally more excited about building expertise, relationships, and the ability to make good decisions later than about trying to get a big, specific policy enacted before we understand what we want.
